statements.quote: Because code is executable, it is the bridge to the symbolic: PAL had the LLM decompose a word problem into a short program and offloaded the computation to an interpreter — a 12B model plus an interpreter beat PaLM-540B's chain-of-thought on GSM8K (\cite[Gao et al., 2022]{gao2022pal}).

Executable code is also a universal action space for agents (up to 20% higher success rates than pre-defined JSON actions \cite[Wang et al., 2024]{wang2024codeact}) and the reason RL with verifiable rewards (see the Reasoning chapter ) works best on code and math: the test suite *is* the reward model.

The lineage: Codex fine-tuned GPT on GitHub code — 28.8% on HumanEval where GPT-3 got 0% (\cite[Chen et al., 2021]{chen2021codex}); Code Llama's 7B Python model, trained on ~500B extra code tokens, beat Llama 2 **70B** on code benchmarks (\cite[Rozière et al., 2023]{roziere2023codellama}); DeepSeek-Coder trained 2T project-level tokens from scratch (\cite[Guo et al., 2024]{guo2024deepseekcoder}).

The other side of the same data: models are strongest where the corpus is thickest — popular languages, mainstream frameworks, English identifiers — and next-token prediction learns surface regularities first, so syntax comes easily while deep semantics (debugging, refactoring) remains the hard part.
The sharpest illustration is **SWE-bench** (\cite[Jimenez et al., 2024]{jimenez2024swebench}), 2,294 real GitHub issues: the best model of 2023 resolved 1.96%.
Reasoning models have since climbed far, but the gap between “passes the unit tests” and “does software engineering” is where the data's limits show.
With natural data exhaust, frontier labs increasingly generate **synthetic training data**:

OpenAI's **WebGPT** and DeepMind's **Sparrow** demonstrated that synthetic preference data can substitute for expensive human labelling, at the cost of ceiling effects (you can't exceed your teacher's quality).
For those training their own models, the rough sequence is:
**Source raw data**: Common Crawl dumps, GitHub, ArXiv, StackExchange, books from public sources.
**Extract text**: HTML → plain text with WARC extraction.
**Language ID**: fastText, keep target languages.
**Quality filter**: heuristic rules + classifier (e.g., FineWeb's quality classifier).
**Deduplicate**: exact hash + MinHash + suffix-array.
**Decontaminate**: against benchmarks you care about.
**Mix and balance**: per-source sampling weights, target ratio (e.g., 50% web, 15% code, 10% books, 5% math).
**Tokenize**: BPE/SentencePiece over a representative sample.

(BPE is a **compression** algorithm from \citeyear{gage1994bpe} \cite{gage1994bpe} repurposed for tokenization: it fuses frequent adjacent pairs into single short-ID tokens, so the token stream is a shorter, lossless form of the raw text.)
**Pack**: concatenate and chunk into fixed-length training sequences.
This pipeline takes weeks of engineering and significant compute.
The result is what you train on.
A famous result from the **DataComp-LM** benchmark: at fixed compute, model quality improves strongly with the **quality-adjusted token count**.

Cleaning the data
Quality Filtering
Web text is mostly junk: SEO spam, machine-translated articles, product listings with 50 keyword variations, “Lorem ipsum”, repetitive template content. A model trained on this learns to mimic junk.

Deduplication
Duplicate or near-duplicate documents **inflate training cost and can cause memorization**. Dedup is essential.

Hash each document (SHA-256 over normalized text); keep only one copy of each hash. Catches verbatim copies but not near-duplicates.
